Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Three protesters scaled the Golden Gate Bridge Monday and unfurled a "Free Tibet" banner, a likely precursor to large protests when the Olympic torch arrives Wednesday in San Francisco, California. Members of Students for a Free Tibet climbed the bridge to place these banners, said the group's spokesman. The banner read, "One World. One Dream. Free Tibet." Those who climbed cables from which the bridge is suspended are members of Students for a Free Tibet, said group spokesman Tenzin Dasang. The three were arrested along with four others at the site. All seven were charged with felony conspiracy and misdemeanor nuisance, said California Highway Patrol Officer Mary Ziegenbein. The climbers also were charged with misdemeanor trespassing.  Watch protesters and banner hung from bridge » . The incident forced the closure of one northbound lane of the bridge. The climbers -- who were on the bridge for about three hours -- came down voluntarily about 1:15 p.m. (4:15 p.m. ET) after workers with the Golden Gate Bridge District began cutting down their banner, Ziegenbein said. Dasang said he has heard of many people planning to protest in San Francisco against China's human rights record. "We want it to be peaceful. But it will be large," said Dasang, 22, during a phone interview in which he said he was near the bridge. "I heard from Tibetans that now live all over the U.S. and even abroad who are coming here." The Olympic flame is on a 130-day journey that will take it through 23 cities on five continents and then throughout China, culminating at the Olympics opening ceremony in Beijing August 8. The San Francisco protest comes the same day as a demonstration in Paris, France, disrupted the torch relay many times. In Paris, police had to cut the Olympic torch relay short Monday amid protests against China's human rights record, French police said. The torch was scheduled to travel 17 miles, past Paris City Hall, but that stop and others were called off after the protests. The torch made it through about 10 miles of its scheduled journey. It was then driven by bus to its final destination, where it was displayed again during a public ceremony at a stadium. Authorities had to play hide-and-seek with the Olympic torch during much of the route, placing it on a bus at least twice during a sometimes chaotic relay route. China has come under international criticism because of its crackdown last month on protesters calling for democratic freedoms and self-rule in Tibet and neighboring Chinese provinces. Protesters have said more than 100 people have died in the crackdown, but Beijing denies that and has accused supporters of the Dalai Lama of orchestrating the violence. U.S. and other Western leaders have called on China to provide civil rights and freedoms to those in Tibet and to enter peaceful discussions aimed at resolving the crisis.  E-mail to a friend .

# Three Golden Rules for Building an Effective CNN

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have revolutionized the field of computer vision, powering everything from facial recognition systems to self-driving cars and medical image analysis. However, designing a CNN that actually performs well requires more than just stacking layers together. Below are three golden rules that can help you build models that are both powerful and reliable.

## The First Golden Rule: Start Simple

One of the most common mistakes beginners make is jumping straight into deep, complex architectures. Instead, the first golden rule is to **start with a simple baseline**. Begin with a modest number of convolutional layers, observe how your model performs, and gradually increase complexity only when needed. This approach helps you understand your data, avoid unnecessary computation, and identify problems early. A simple model that works is always better than a complicated one you can't debug.

## The Second Golden Rule: Respect Your Data

The second golden rule is that **data quality matters more than architecture**. Even the most sophisticated CNN will fail if it's trained on poor, unbalanced, or noisy data. Invest time in cleaning your dataset, applying meaningful data augmentation, and ensuring your classes are well represented. Techniques like flipping, cropping, and normalizing images can dramatically improve a model's ability to generalize. Remember: a CNN only learns what you show it.

## The Third Golden Rule: Regularize and Validate

The third golden rule is to **always guard against overfitting**. Powerful networks can easily memorize training data instead of learning general patterns. Use techniques such as dropout, batch normalization, and early stopping to keep your model honest. Just as importantly, validate your results on data the model has never seen. Reliable evaluation is what separates a model that looks good on paper from one that works in the real world.

## Conclusion

Building a successful CNN is as much an art as it is a science. By following these three golden rules—starting simple, respecting your data, and regularizing carefully—you set yourself up for models that are efficient, accurate, and trustworthy. Whether you're a student experimenting with your first network or a professional deploying systems at scale, these principles will serve as a solid foundation for your work.

# Protesters Scale Golden Gate Bridge in 'Free Tibet' Demonstration Ahead of Olympic Torch

**SAN FRANCISCO** — Pro-Tibet activists climbed the suspension cables of the Golden Gate Bridge on Monday, unfurling banners protesting China's human rights record just days before the Olympic torch was scheduled to make its only North American appearance in San Francisco.

Three demonstrators scaled the iconic bridge's cables early in the morning, hanging two large banners reading "One World, One Dream, Free Tibet" and "Free Tibet '08" — a pointed reference to Beijing's official Olympic slogan, "One World, One Dream."

## Dramatic Protest Draws International Attention

The activists, affiliated with the group Students for a Free Tibet, remained suspended more than 100 feet above the bridge's roadway for several hours as authorities worked to bring them down safely.

"We wanted to send a message to the world that the Olympic Games cannot proceed while the people of Tibet are being oppressed," one organizer told reporters at the scene.

The demonstration comes amid heightened tensions following unrest in Tibet, where protests against Chinese rule earlier in the spring were met with a government crackdown. The events have galvanized activists worldwide who are using the Olympic torch relay as a platform to draw attention to their cause.

## Authorities Respond

The California Highway Patrol and San Francisco emergency crews responded to the scene. Several protesters were taken into custody after being brought down from the bridge. Officials emphasized that public safety was their primary concern given the dangerous heights involved.

The Golden Gate Bridge, one of the most recognizable landmarks in the United States, provided a highly visible backdrop that ensured the demonstration would capture media attention around the globe.

## Bracing for the Torch Relay

The protest set the stage for what officials anticipate could be contentious scenes when the Olympic flame arrives in San Francisco. The city represents the torch's only stop in North America on its international journey to Beijing.

The relay has faced disruptions in other cities, with demonstrators in London and Paris attempting to interfere with the flame's progress. In Paris, the torch was reportedly extinguished multiple times amid the chaos.

San Francisco officials have said they are preparing security measures for the torch's arrival while working to balance public safety with the rights of demonstrators to express their views.

## A Divisive Global Moment

The Beijing Olympics, intended to showcase China's emergence as a global power, have instead become a lightning rod for critics of the Chinese government's policies on Tibet, human rights, and other issues.

Chinese officials have condemned the protests as attempts to politicize the Games and disrupt an event meant to unite nations.

As the torch makes its way toward San Francisco, city leaders, activists, and law enforcement are all preparing for a day that could bring the world's competing narratives about the Beijing Games into sharp focus.

*This is a developing story.*

# 2008 Olympic Torch Relay Sparks Global Protests Over Tibet, Human Rights

## International Journeys of the Olympic Flame Meet Widespread Demonstrations

The 2008 Summer Olympics torch relay, intended as a celebratory prelude to the Beijing Games, became a flashpoint for international protests as demonstrators across multiple cities challenged China's human rights record, particularly regarding its policies in Tibet.

## Paris: Torch Extinguished Amid Chaos

In Paris on April 7, 2008, the torch relay descended into disarray as thousands of protesters lined the route. French authorities deployed thousands of police officers, but demonstrations grew so intense that the torch was reportedly extinguished multiple times and forced onto a bus for portions of the journey.

**Key events in Paris included:**

- Pro-Tibet activists attempted to disrupt the relay near the Eiffel Tower
- Protesters displayed Tibetan flags and banners referencing human rights concerns
- The flame's passage was significantly altered, with some segments canceled
- French officials faced criticism for the security challenges

The Paris City Hall reportedly hung a banner supporting human rights, and the planned reception at the city hall was among events affected by the tensions.

## San Francisco: The Only North American Stop

San Francisco held the distinction of being the sole North American city on the torch's route. On April 9, 2008, city officials, anticipating disruptions, made last-minute changes to the planned route.

**Notable developments in San Francisco:**

- The route was dramatically altered without advance notice to the public
- The torch was diverted away from crowds who had gathered along the originally announced path
- Both pro-Tibet demonstrators and pro-China supporters assembled in significant numbers
- The closing ceremony location was changed, and the torch was taken to the airport rather than completing a public celebration

Then-Mayor Gavin Newsom's administration faced criticism from multiple sides—protesters felt silenced, while others questioned the handling of the event.

## Broader Context

The protests reflected international attention on several issues:

- **Tibet:** Unrest in Tibet earlier in 2008 had drawn global scrutiny
- **Human rights concerns:** Various advocacy groups raised broader issues
- **Darfur:** Some activists connected China's foreign policy to the conflict in Sudan

## Reactions

The demonstrations prompted varied responses. Chinese officials and many Chinese citizens viewed the protests as unwelcome politicization of the Olympics. Advocacy organizations, including those supporting Tibetan autonomy, characterized the relay as an opportunity to raise awareness.

The torch relay's difficulties in Paris and San Francisco, along with disruptions in London and other cities, led organizers to reconsider aspects of the international relay's remaining route.

# Activists Scale Bridge in Tibet Solidarity Protest; Multiple Arrests Reported

**By Staff Writer**

Traffic slowed and onlookers gathered Tuesday morning as a group of activists scaled a support tower on a major California bridge, unfurling banners calling for Tibetan independence in a demonstration organized by the advocacy group Students for a Free Tibet.

The protest, which began shortly after 7 a.m., saw several demonstrators climb roughly 150 feet up the bridge's cabling before securing themselves and displaying banners reading "Free Tibet" and "China: Stop the Occupation." The banners remained visible for several hours as authorities worked to bring the activists down safely.

## Activists Cite Human Rights Concerns

Tenzin Dolma, a spokesperson for Students for a Free Tibet, defended the demonstration as a necessary act of civil disobedience aimed at drawing international attention to conditions inside Tibet.

"We understand that our actions caused disruption today, and we don't take that lightly," Dolma said. "But the people of Tibet have endured decades of disruption to their lives, their culture, and their basic freedoms. Sometimes it takes a bold action to make the world pay attention to voices that are being silenced."

Dolma added that the group had planned the demonstration carefully to prioritize safety. "Our activists are experienced climbers, and our goal was never to endanger anyone. We wanted to be heard, not to harm."

## Law Enforcement Responds

The California Highway Patrol coordinated the response, closing several lanes as officers and specialized rescue crews worked to safely remove the demonstrators.

"Our primary concern throughout this incident was the safety of everyone involved—the individuals on the structure, our officers, and the motoring public," said CHP Officer Michael Reyes. "These types of demonstrations create significant hazards, both for the participants and for drivers who may be distracted by the activity overhead."

Reyes noted that the lane closures contributed to substantial traffic delays during the morning commute. "We appreciate the public's patience while our teams resolved the situation without any injuries."

## Arrests and Charges

According to the CHP, six individuals were taken into custody after being brought down from the bridge structure. Officers reported that the activists cooperated during the removal process.

Those arrested face charges including trespassing, creating a public nuisance, and unlawfully causing a traffic obstruction, Reyes said. Additional charges related to public safety may be pursued as the investigation continues.

"Peaceful expression is a protected right, but climbing critical infrastructure crosses a line into criminal conduct that puts lives at risk," Reyes said.

Dolma said the group was prepared for the legal consequences. "Our activists knew there might be arrests, and they accepted that responsibility. We believe history will judge who was truly on the right side of this issue."

The demonstrators were booked at a nearby county facility, and all lanes reopened by early afternoon. The CHP said it does not anticipate lasting structural concerns to the bridge.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

# Global Torch Relay Marred by Protests as Beijing Olympics Approach

*Demonstrations follow Olympic flame across continents amid tensions over Tibet*

The 2008 Olympic torch relay, billed by organizers as a celebration of international unity, has instead become a flashpoint for protest as the flame makes its way toward the Beijing Summer Games.

## An Ambitious Journey

Chinese organizers designed the relay as the longest in Olympic history, a 130-day journey covering approximately 137,000 kilometers across five continents before the flame's arrival at the opening ceremony in Beijing. The route, which included a controversial planned ascent of Mount Everest, was intended to showcase China's emergence as a global power and its readiness to host the world.

Instead, the relay has drawn demonstrators to city streets from London to Paris to San Francisco.

## Protests Erupt Across Continents

In several Western cities, the torch's passage has been met with significant demonstrations. In Paris, security concerns reportedly forced officials to extinguish the flame multiple times as protesters attempted to disrupt the route. London saw scuffles between demonstrators and security personnel accompanying the torch, while San Francisco organizers altered the announced route to avoid crowds.

Protesters have raised a range of grievances, with many focusing on human rights concerns and China's policies in Tibet.

## Unrest in Tibet

The demonstrations follow a period of heightened tension in Tibet, where protests earlier in the year led to a security crackdown by Chinese authorities. Reports of the unrest and the subsequent response drew international attention and criticism from human rights organizations, though accounts of casualties and the scale of the crackdown varied, and independent verification proved difficult given restrictions on journalists' access to the region.

Chinese officials characterized the situation as a matter of internal security and maintained that their response was aimed at restoring order.

## Divergent Responses

The protests have placed governments and Olympic officials in a difficult position. Some world leaders faced pressure over whether to attend the opening ceremony, while the International Olympic Committee expressed concern about the politicization of the relay but reaffirmed its commitment to the Games.

Chinese authorities and many Chinese citizens, meanwhile, expressed frustration at what they viewed as attempts to tarnish a moment of national pride, with some organizing counter-demonstrations in support of the Games.

## Looking Ahead

As the torch continues toward Beijing, the controversies surrounding the relay have underscored the complex intersection of sports, politics, and international relations that the Games have come to represent.

---

*This article is written in a general journalistic style for illustrative purposes. Readers seeking detailed accounts of specific events should consult contemporary news archives and multiple sources.*
